chapter: Harlem, Redman's band and the Savoy
title: Rex Stewart's tricks, appetite and reading
summary: Rex Stewart had many tricks and false fingerings, a big appetite and a good ear that covered slow reading; Jackson played with him in McKinney's band.

story.theme_name: Remembering the early trumpeters and their styles
story.community_name: Trumpeters I admired: rating the horn players

blocks.x: But since we're on the trumpet players of yesteryear, and I know you've met some of them and I've heard so much about some of them and knew some of them with you, can you tell us a little about Rex Stewart?
Rex Stewart was one of the most fantastic trumpet players that I've ever known. He had so

many tricks and he was fast, very fast. You know, that's who Roy listened to in the beginning. That's who Roy kind of patterned after to adopt his style, you see. And Rex used to cover the valves up -- he would finger his horn and cover the valves up and use a lot of false fingering so the guys couldn't tell what he was doing, you know. And a very -- he had an enormous appetite.

Oh, yes, he did. But he wasn't a real fast reader either. They found that out in Duke's band. But he had such a good ear, too, you know. They'd bring the music in for their parts out there and Tizol used to turn around and tell him, "uh-uh, I heard what you played there," because Tizol had did the copying, you know.
But once he got it down, though, he could play. He was fantastic. He had a lot of tricks, to me. A lot of tricks. He --
Did you ever get to play with him at any time?
Sure. I got to play with him then and that's when I really found out, you know. He has a solo on the record I sang on, "Do You Believe in Love at Sight?"
He has a record -- he has a solo on there. And Bennie Carter made that arrangement, by the way.
